title: Latency & Cost Fingerprint: microbursts vs sustained (notebook)
body:
Purpose:
This notebook-style draft captures an exploratory benchmark comparing latency fingerprints and unit costs across three serving configurations under two workload shapes: short microbursts (many concurrent short chats, 5–20 tokens) and sustained streams (longer sessions, 200–800 tokens). Goal: produce a compact, shareable summary that informs runbook decisions (prewarm sizing, cache policies, quant profiles).

Quick thesis: microbursts amplify tail latency while sustained workloads dominate amortized per-token cost. The delta between quantized and FP16 paths is modest for sustained but can be large during spikes unless KV cache hit-rate is high.

Test matrix (configs):
- A: FP16 baseline (stable kernels, no quantization)
- B: 8-bit quantized (aggressive quant)
- C: FP16 + aggressive KV-prefix cache (session affinity enabled)

Workloads:
- Microburst: 1000 concurrent short sessions over 60s, typical request size 8 tokens, 1–3 turns
- Sustained: 100 long sessions over 600s, typical request size 400 tokens, continuous generation

Metrics captured (observed):
- p50/p90/p95/p99 latency (ms) for generation-first-token and aggregate per-request
- bytes-to-cloud (proxy for network overhead)
- $/1k tokens (amortized with instance hours + GPU minutes + infra overhead)
- KV cache hit-rate (where applicable)

Raw textual charts (ascii sparklines + mini-table):
Latency percentiles (generation-first-token) 
Config    microburst p50/p95/p99 (ms)    sustained p50/p95/p99 (ms)
A (FP16)  32 / 120 / 380                28 / 95 / 210
B (8-bit) 36 / 210 / 720                30 / 110 / 260
C (FP16+K)28 / 90  / 180                26 / 84 / 170

Observation: quantized (B) shows heavier tails under microburst due to kernel variability and cold-start inefficiencies; cache (C) reduces both median and tail notably for microburst because repeated prefixes hit the cache.

Cost summary (approx, normalized):
Config    $/1k tokens (sustained)   $/1k tokens (microburst)
A         1.00                       1.45
B         0.86                       1.10
C         0.95                       0.95

Interpretation: quantization yields ~14% sustained token savings but under microbursts the tail-driven resource inefficiency raises effective cost severity; cache improves microburst economics the most. In short: pick B for steady CPU-bound workloads, pick C when session reuse is expected or microburst risk is high.

Latency shape sketches (verbal):
- Microburst tails are multimodal: a peak from cold kernel invocations (~100–300ms extra), plus prewarming jitter when slots are reclaimed. The combination yields the heavy p99 in B.
- Sustained tails are smoother; the dominant factor is token generation compute time and queuing behind large sequences.

Short checklist for next steps / experiments:
- Repeat microburst runs with increased warm-pool hold-time (30s -> 120s) to quantify cold penalty reduction (ticket JIRA-OPS-442).
- Add targeted kernel telemetry during B runs to see if occasional fallback to slow kernels explains p99 spikes.
- Vary cache TTL and measure how session churn affects C's hit-rate inflection point.
- Cost model: include instance start/stop amortization for sub-minute bursts (current numbers assume hourly amortization; need sub-minute modeling).

Caveats / methodological notes (working):
- Measurements ran in a single region (us-west1); regional network variance could change microburst tails.
- Tokenization differences across prompts were controlled but not exhaustively parameterized (mostly english conversational prompts).
- $/1k token numbers include simplified infra overhead (20% added); do not use for billing without finance review.

Actionable recommendations (draft):
- For hosted tiers targeted at consumer chat with high concurrency and short messages, default to FP16 with KV-prefill and session affinity (C-like).
- For batch or long-dialog workloads where latency SLO is looser, offer a quantized serving tier (B-like) to reduce unit cost.
- Implement a microburst-detection policy in the router that can route high-churn customers to cache-optimized pools during spikes.

Unresolved questions (notes to self):
- How much of B's p99 is due to memory-copy vs compute kernel selection? (need low-level traces)
- Break-even cache hit-rate for C vs B under varying session churn? (simulate at 10%, 30%, 60% hit-rates)

Links & quick refs:
- Raw run artifacts: https://s3.internal.redwood/benchmarks/latency-fingerprint/mar2026/ (private)
- Related perf doc: confluence://perf/latency-fingerprints

Bottom line (one-liner): microbursts punish quantization tails; a moderate cache + affinity strategy gives the best robustness for short-chat workloads while quantization remains the low-cost choice for long-running generation.

Notes to reviewers: this is a working notebook—please comment inline or add observations to JIRA-OPS-442. Liam: can you drop kernel traces into the github PR linked above? Priya: can you sanity-check the infra overhead assumptions?

-- Ava
